goldens.comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
goldens.reasoning: C1 points out the stats side effects during a check/validation. C4 points out the race condition in the stats update. G1 raises both concerns.

goldens.comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.
goldens.reasoning: None of the candidates mention the regex domain-boundary bypass.

goldens.comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
goldens.reasoning: C2 identifies the same case-sensitivity bypass.

candidates: Email validation calls BlockedEmail.should_block? which increments match_count and saves, causing DB writes during validation - UsersController#create runs validations at least twice (valid? then save), so a single blocked signup attempt will double-increment stats and add unnecessary DB write load

BlockedEmail lookup uses exact string match, so case/whitespace variants of a blocked address can bypass blocking and allow duplicate blocked entries differing only by case - should canonicalize via Email.downcase(...).strip like other email lookups
EmailValidator always queries BlockedEmail which will raise an exception if the new blocked_emails table hasn't been migrated yet during deploy - should use table_exists? guard pattern
BlockedEmail.should_block? updates match_count by read-modify-write which can lose increments under concurrent requests - should be incremented atomically
